The Boston I'ost contains an aide article embracing a very full and detailed account of the copper mines on the southern shore of Lake Sugenor, the manner of working them, and the progress which has thus far been made in getting out the ore by the different companies. The sudden importance which this trade has acquired, and the gieat influence w hich it will soon exercise on the commerce of the United States, renders all information on the subject interesting. The article is too long to copy entire, but we subjoin the follow ing extracts : The copper region commences at Chocolate River, a little East of Copper harbor, in l.ake Superior, and extends along the Southern shore some 3(5t) miles to the British line, pursuing a north westerly direction. The width is from I to 25 miles, according to the course of the ranges of trap rock, tfie uniform concomitant of the ore. This region abounds in evidence of ancient volr.anious action, particularly in the frequent appearance among the ore of bodies of native copper. The ore

appears in veins on the surface of the earth and in rocks on the lull sides. Those veins vary in width from 0 to Iff feel. Some of them descend into the earth perpendicularly, others at various degrees of inclination, and some of them, after performing a enrviture under the earth, re appear ' crop out' again. The ores yield on an average, about 25 per cent, of pure copper þÿ the purest in the world. The mines of Cornwall in England, yield onlv from 8 to 9 per cent; those of Bohemia about 15. The only mines in the world þÿ except those of Cuba and Jamaica, of which we are ignorant þÿ that rival in richness the mines of Lake Superior are those of Russia. The latter are also the only ones which are worked with equal facility, being like the Superior mines, near the surface, aud yield-

S It D I z; AT ITS. ing, from the very commencement of opera lion, ample supplies of metal The mines of Cornwall and Hungary are worked to the depth of 25000 feet, aud in some casus the first 500 lee l have been excavated at an expense of $300 000 to half a million, before any thing was realized. No shaft ori Lake Superior has as yet been sunk to a greater depth than 100 feet. It is leinarkuble that a copper vein never fails unless it ctops out elsewhere. Interruptions, faults mov occur, but continued digging will strike the ore again. The cost of getting ore to the surface is about four dollars per ton, one liuud being able to get out about half a ton per day 1 tie coasting or washing, so far, is about half that price þÿ say altogether about six dollars per ton. II the ore yield 25 per cent of metal, it is worth, at 10 cents per pound, eighty dollars ; thus leaving a large margin for these articles to bear a duty of 30 pr. ct. þÿ profit, after the expense for working the mines ate paid. Such operations have, of course, attracted operators, who have proceeded with equal celerity and silence to explore and appropriate tire localities ulioidmg ine best indications of metal. Our Government, so far, has adopted ihe policy of leasing, a- tirst in tracts of nine miles square, now of only one. The leases continue tor nine years, at a rate of six per cent, of the ore for tfie first tluee years, and ten per cent for the residue of the period the tenant giving secui ity for the due payment of the share, and renewing the bond

every tlnee years. Operations were commenced by two companies in 1814. In 1845 twelve more companies have begun working. The location of these companies have been generally in the neighborhood of Copper Harbor, on Kewanu l'oinl ; those selections having been made not oniy for the appaieni superiority in the quantity of ore, but from the convenience to navigation, so iluit supplies of provisions and hands can tie easily procured, and the ore or metal be cheaply transported to market. The two companies which commenced in 1814, are now ready with ores for smelting or washing. The Lake Superior Company has 1100 tons on hand. The 1'itisburgh and Boston some 100 tons, having been extensively engaged in preparations. We understand that it requires but a small þÿsum some 3 or 81000 þÿ to commence these operations in mining profitably ; although, perhaps, much larger suins might he advantageously employed. The Companies already formed, however, not being under the necessity of making great outlays, nor of waiting long for returns, will not be compelled to force large quantities of stock on the market, and will be able to realize for themselves the fruit of that sagacity and energy that have given them the lead in this undertaking. We almost forget to state that the Lake Superior Company, at Eagle river, the Supetior Company near Copper Harbor, and the Ontonagon, on the Elm river, have found in their ores a large proportion of silver, a quantity so great as to yield on its separation
from ihe copper an additional profit greater than that of the copper itself. þÿ N. Y. Bnper.

INDUSTRY. Nothing can he accomplished without labor, the merchant cannot thrive, mechanic cannot gain his support, n < r the beggar his victuals. Every thing in our outset in life depends in a great measure upon the activity and energy of the mind for its ultimate success. Our relations to mankind and to society, render it an imperative obligation on us to oe engaged in some useful employment, if it be but in sustaining our own existence, or in seeking pleasure, no matter, (lie obligation is the same. There is no greater curse to the world than a drone His example counterbalances all Ins lessons or precepits of good, and thereby neutralises their effect. But if for no other reason, we should he engaged in active employment " for our own cause for our health; the improvement of the physical, as well as mental constitution ; and for pleasure. Activity gives a healthful tone to the blood, muscles and brain, clearness of thought and perception to the mind. It makes life a pleasure rather than a burden, and lengthens it to good old age. The idle man cannot be a philosopher. Nature may have done alt necessary for him, but she wants assisting þÿ The wisenian is the active man : the business man, the states man, the hero, and the man of literary honor, have all arrived at their siations in society, not bv supinencss and idleness, hut by activity and zeal.

Execution of Thomas Posset. ( Condemned for murder on the High Sens Thomas Posset, whose name w ill bo remembered lor many revolving years in this community, expiated the nwlul and diabolical crime of which he had been convicted, on Thursday morning last. The wretched criminal was brought out from Ins prison a little alter sur.tise, and taken in a cart, guarded by the military, to the jitnce of execution, He appeared perfectly calm and collected during the whole ol the progress of the melancholy procession. He sat on a bench (heing finely bound; in the centre of the Cart, and by Ins side the Rev'd. Mr. Alignon, Catholic Priest, to whose exhortations as the vehicle of death slowly wended its mournful way þÿ he appeared to pay the most profound attention. Liehind the reverend gentleman and the doonied man, the executioner, sat, or rather squatted on the lioor ol the cart. The criminal was clothed in white and appeared much broken by his long confinement, and the sufferings he must have undergone from the wounds he received when captured after his escape liom his prison on the night of the :id March last year. On teaching the foot id the lull, in which the scad Id was elected, the Priest, the criminal, and executioner, alighted, and walked slowly up the ascent, in consequence ot the lameness ol I'osset. On arriving at the ladder leading up to the platform, lie knelt, and the Priest bestowing on him his parting Benediction, retired from the distressing scene. As he rose from his knees, lie stood up and listened to his sentence of con-

demnation, which was read unto him, and he then followed the executioner up the ladder, and as he slept on the platform turned round and respectfully but collectedly lequesied permission to say a few wotds to those atound. He spoke as nearly as we couid gather to the following etleo.t, fur the sobs and lamentations Irom the assembled crowd, a great portion of whom weie women, ren dered it extremely difficult to catch Ins words although he spoke audibly and (irmly. He said "look at me, take warning from poor " Thomas I'osset, don't cry, hut pray in all "the churches for me, I'm going to die with "God in my heart, goodbye, my brothers ' and sisters, good bye." These words were accompanied by emphatic gestures, bowing and waving his hands as he turned from side to sole, and addressed Ihcm to the spectators. When he had limshed speaking he took his station beneath the fatal drop. The execu tioner adjusted tiie þÿnoose the trap fell þÿ and after several convulsive struggles, for he died very hard, from being of a most poweiful frame þÿ his guilty soul winged its wav to the judgment seat before which murderers and victims must all appear. The body hung till sunset when it was cut down and interred close by the retributive tree on which lie atoned in this world for his crime. We have refrained during the long period of incarnation of Tlios Fosse I from giving any account, or particulars of the crime for which he was under prosecution, as we were unable during that time to learn aught, hut

from rumours and reports as they were current. and were unwilling to mislead the pub lie mind, or in any way prejudge a case pending before the tribunals. He is now however uo mote, he has paid the penalty ul

amume ' " ii 1 1 tm the law, and the following details ol his crime extracted bv permission of the autluu ities from the public books, w title they will excite a painful intetest, may, ori the other band, coupled with his awful fate serve as a warning voice to those who may be lempttd to forget the (iat, " Whoso' slx-diietli man's blood, by man shall Ins blood be shed " On the 27th December 1844, the police master was informed that a free black man 1 horn as Losset. had arrived in this city on the evening previous, and that he had asserted that the Danish sloop Caroline in which he sailed was stranded, and that three Spaniards, the Captain, a sailor and u passenger were drowned. Fossei's reputation was so notoriously bad, and the circumstances as stated to have been related by htm so singular, tfiat suspicion was immediately aroused, thai both murder and robbery might have been committed. i'reliminarv steps were immediately taken to discover the truth of these statements, and it was ascertained that Fosset trad brought with him a number of tilings from the stranded vessel, viz: a barrel of beef or pork, some bundles with pieces of clothing and other things, and moreover, (which confirmed lire suspicions already excited) that he the said Fosset had rowed out of the harbour in a boat, on the morning of the 27th without having given any tnlormation of what find occurred, either to the government or police. The wlnde of that day a fruitless search was made lor the vessel which was ali'Twarus found to have been stranded in a

nook in Frenchman's Bay, but tie was discovered the same evening by one of the police at the entrance of the harbour. An old free black iiihii bv name Theodore Scobald and himself were rowing the boat, which contained also, a barrel of flour, a quantity of salted meat and different pieces of clothing and other things, and both Thus. Fosset aid Theodore ISc.obald were arrested. 'That it w as his intention to conceal the articles found with him in the boat, of which he must have fraudulently possessed himself, as with tire exception of a few and very trifling things they belonged to t fie Spaniards, whom he insisted had been accidentally drowned, was evident, as he had made no proper report or announcement of the loss of the vessel, and the lives ol the Spaniards, and because he brought them ashore late in the evening, and had threatened to beat the woman with whom he lived if she did not conceal those things which fie had brought on shore the day previous from the stranded vessel and had given her to keep. A preliminary Court was field on the day following at which I heodore Scobald declared without circumlocution, oi equivocation, that Thomas Fosset had murdered the three Spaniards who weie on board the sloop Caroline arid left. St. Croix on December 24th, bound for Crab island, 'l'lie names of the three Spaniards who were inhumanely murdered were Raymond Morales, the Captain of the sloop, Juan a seaman, and Capiiano Cordero, a passenger. According to the declaration of Theodore

Scohald, Fosset had succeeded iu efl etiog his murderous design by suddenly striking violently, the two first mentioned on tin: head with the back <4 an axe as thev lav sleeping on the deck, until they no longer showed signs of life, and that then he threw the bodies overboard. The third Spaniard, t'npitatiu Cordero, who was sleeping heiow, was

þÿr þÿ»T aroused by the noise and came on deck, and that as Fosset saw him he rushed towards him with the axe in his hand þÿ and the spa niard in his fright jumped overboard, after which the three were never seen again. The foregoing evidence of I heodore Scobald, the witness for tire Grown was met on the part of Fosset, not by denial, for he admitted that lie had killed the three Spaniards, but as he averred in his own defence. Several courts were held from time to time after this, at which the same charge on the part of the crown witness was adhered to, and the same line of defence pertinaciously insisted on by the criminal, and there existed little likelihood of his guilt being legally proved, as our Laws require two credible witnesses of a crime prior to condemnation, up to the period of his escape from the cell of his prison in which he was chained. This occurrence took place on Monday night March 3rd 1H45. He had succeeded in releasing himself from his chains by breaking the padlock þÿ and having done so, made a noise which attracted the attention of the sentinel on duty who reported it, and the goaler and a serjeant proceeded to the cell to ascertain the cause of the uproar. On unlocking the door, Fosset who must have been watching the critical moment, struck at them furiously with the chain he held in his hand and succeeded in passing them. Rushing at the sentinel he passed him also, hut in the seuifle received n bayonet wound in the side. He then ran to the sea side and plunged into the warnr. An alarm

was fired insianter, and in a few moments the city so quiet before was literally alive. The Militia were promptly at their posts and the moment the cause of the alarm was ascertained, hundreds were aiding the authorities, military and police in recapturing the fugitive. For full two hours he baffled his pursuers, by swimming from whirl to wharf and hiding among the piles, but he was at length captured, and reconducted to prison half dead with the fatigue, wounds and bruises lie had received in his un-ticccssful attempt to escape from the iron hand of Justice. Un the morning of the f>th from remorse of conscience in all probability, dreading that he was about to die, he signified his desire of making h full confession of his guilt, which confession during the remainder of his confinement he adhered to, up to the morning of his death, never once signifying that lie retracted an ioUi of tiie facts, as contained in his confession : þÿ FUSS UTS CONFESSION. In the year 1 813 on the 5th of March in the forenoon at 10 o'clock, a St. 1 homas Extra Court was held in Christians' Fort and administered by the undersigned in presence of the sheriff and witnesses Schmaltz and Toiisen, where and when was undertaken the suit No. 1. 1845. The prisoner Thomas I'osset appeared (unshackled) before the Court, who then made the following confessions That when he shipped himself on board the sloop Caroline, he had premeditated to wreak his revenge for the injustice which he considered he had suffered in not having been

accepted "I, as owner of the said vessel. The thought of committing some evil had long lain nurtured in his mind, and his indignation had now risen to its utmost pitch, as he was obliged to work harder than the oiher wtio left the pumping of the vessel entirely to him, while they were laying at their ease on deck,

Although the deponent asserts, that revenge and hatred really actuated bun to commit three murders, and which

he bitterly repents, yet he cannot deny, that he, at the same lime, thought of putting himself in possession of their property, alter having murdered them, as he subsequently did, but he assures that he found no money, and if they have had money with them, they must huvu but tie it upon their persons as he did not search their pockets, alter killing them. The deponent left the axe, with which he had killed lite Spaniards, on hoard, it was a large axe, one which is used to chop wood. This confession was read to the prisoner which he declared to he truth and thus revokes all foiegoing declarations, which do not corroborate with this. The prisoner was again delivered lo the guard. confidence in Seoba Id as being ( tie of his ow n " Caste," that he felt assured he w< old not be betrayed bv him. Again ! to what ate we to attribute his remorse and voluntary confession þÿ certainly not to a cowardly and broken spirit, lor no man could have met his doom more caltnlv or more firmly, or have evinced less of ihe braggart on the awful occasion, ret us hope, that in those solitary communings he must have had with his conscience, that God softened his sinful heart and rendered him in spirit and in notti a penitent ; and that seeing clearly the enormity of the' crimes with which he had stained his guilty soul, he surrendered himself to the penalty attached to all who violate the commandment : " Thou shall do no murder," and that he did so in the hope; ihai bv humbly and penitently submiting to the decree of the Eternal "Forgive, ness might be exLended to him beyond the grave."

NAPOLEON AND THE GRENADIER. It was after the battle of Jena that the emperor entered the capital of the Prussian dominions in triumph. In a short tunc he left Berlin with his staff", of which 1 was a member. Several detachments of the French were in full march, so thai the road from Berlin to lvonigsburg was ciowded with soldiers, waggons, artillery and the baggage train. '1 be emperor, as was bis custom, took the bye roads, arid travelled so fast that but few could keep up with hiin. The soldiers who saw him pass by, accompanied only by two or three officers, gave liim the nickname of the ' petit corporal !" Being pretty well mounted, I generally managed to keep pace with him, and thus had an opportunity of remarking that he sometimes looked behind to know who was following : and he could not help smiling when he remarked how few there were in his train. The heavy rains however, impeded our march, anci it was with some difficulty ihat we were able to advance at all in some [daces All at once the emperor reined op his horse to look at a grenadier of noble figuie with black moustaches and whiskers, sitting under n tree, his musket, knapsack and large enp by his side, and who was busily engaged in roasting a potato on some ashes which were yet burning. He was so intent on his occupation, that he neither saw the emperor or the troops marching by him. After watching him for some moments, the emperor s aid, Hailo, grenadier, what are you doing there? That's a pretty question, answered the grenadier, with a broad Gas-

con accent, a man musi be blind not to see that I am roasting a potato on the point of my knife. Thai's true, replied Napoleon ; here give it me I'm hungry. Ah, ah ! that's good ? give it to you ! give it to \ou ! Not such a fool as that ! 1 am roasting it foi mvself and not for others. I am hungry ! and he imitated the emperor's voice so well that we could not help laughing. Come here's a gold piece ; give me hall of it 1 don't want your gold ; can 1 eat it ? will it satisfy mv hunger ? Bonaparte was much astonished at his refusal and asked him authoritatively if he knew who he was speaking to. He, still seated, and very busily occupied in turning Ins potato, looked up at him and replied. Humph ! do I know to whom I am speaking? To a man. I hope ; not to a God or a devil. But I enquire if you know me þÿ if you are aware to whom you are speaking? Who you are ? Yes! no doubt I know you well þÿ you are our "petit corporal !" and a good fellow ; hut you shan't have mv potato for I am hungry So saving, he drew it deliberately from the ashes, and added in the same quiet and easy manner, Egad, 1 think it will soon be done ! The en peror could not help smiling, and said in a milder tone, come niv good fellow, 1 have a proposition to make to you ; if you will give me half your potato you shall come aud dine with me this evening. What? are you in earnest? dine with you for half mv þÿpotato? ha. ha, ha, þÿ agreed ! þÿ the proposal is a good one I accept it But come I hope you are not joking, and that

you won't laugh at me alter having cat half of my potato. Beware of that for " Bras de for is in earnest. No, no. replied the Emperor, laughing, pledge you mv word I That's enough said the grenadier quite dc

«r ir - i þÿ ' 1 Ti lighted, at the same time giving him half his potato which he had fixed on the point of his bayonet, and thus handed it to the emperor, who took it and eat it ohseiving that it vvas verv good. We continued our march and on the road Napoleon asked us if we knew who that queer fellow was, or his name. None of us could give the desired information, so the matter dropped. In the evening, just as we were sitting down to tahle, a noise was heard in the ante chamber, and many voices speaking together in anger. The emperor surprised at this enquired what was the matter, when a servant came in, saving there was an insolent soldier outside, all covered with mud and dirt, who having made Ins way as tar as the ante chamber, was enquiring it his majesty was at home, and that he had come to dine wiih him on his invitation ; and, added the servant, when we laughed at tins, and told him he could not come in, he abused us, called us impude: t footmen, robbers, scamps, and persisted in his determination ol seeing your majesty. At this information we most of us laughed and reminded the emperor of Ins morning's adventure. lie immediately entered him in. Our hero entered in full marching costume, and presenting arms marched straight to the emperor, who was seated at the centre of the table, balled, presented arms like an orderly giving or receiving a report and looking the emperor lull in 'he face, said boldly, !Sire, hero 1 am þÿ Bras do fer. þÿ grenadier in the 12th regt. of the line. I shared my breakfast with you

on condition that I should dine with you. It was vour own proposal, and I accepted it, after a forced and rapid march here 1 am, and as every honest man keeps his word 1 suppose von mean to. Certainly niv man. vou are right. Here, Constant, take care of this brave fellow, and give him a good dinner- Go, my friend, my valet will take good care of vou Bras de fer knit his black eye brows ; he first looked at the emperor and then with a contemptuous sneer at Iris valet, who was beckoning him to follow, and then looked round at us all. Come, grenadier, cried the emperor impatiently, he oil þÿ go and dine with Constant; I have told you lie will take good care of you. General answered he firmly, I wear a uniform, and cannot dine with valets. 1 must confess this noble answer gratified me, but 1 began to fear so hold a reply might displease Napoleon. In fact, he turned in anger towards the grenadier, who returned his glance without betraying either fear or surprise. Napoleon however soon recovered himself changed his tone and þÿ You are right my brave fellow, and rotir opinion is correct ; put down your musket, take off your knapsack, and sit down by niv side. That's right replied the other, that's what 1 call talking like an emperor! lie then made a halt turn, grounded his musket like a sentry on duty, and as the servants hastened officiously to assist hint in disencumbering himself of his accoutrements, he said to them, loud enough to be heard by us all þÿ lie off with veu, and leave me alone ! þÿ

Having divested himself of his arms Ate , he advanced to the emperor, and raising his hand to his forshead, said Your orders, General. This sallv created a loud laugh, in which the emperor joined, and it had the effect of restoring him to perfect good humour. In the mean time, a knife and fork had been laid by the emperor's side, who

The emperor, who like the rest of us was much amused hv the man's easy, frank and comical manners, helped him with his own hands to every thing lie wished to eat, and made him drink in proportion. He asked him many questions, which he did not stop to answer except by monosyllables At last, wearied with Ins exertions, having eaten enough for six ordinary men, and drank proportionately, he turned round to the emperor, arid said : Now, sire 1 am able to answer anv questions that you may please to put to me. He then told us tiiat he had been with Bonaparte the two last Italian campaigns, had been with him to Egypt; was there left for dead at (Juno, Arc. He then rose, opened Ins knapsack, and handed the emperor his papers and certificates, who on dismissing lum said he would have them examined ; and he might expect shortly to hear Irotn him. Two day's after, he received the cross ol trie legion ol honour, and a captain's commission. His name was Charles Bidot. 1 have not since heard of him, nor do I know what afterwards became of him.

On approaching the roads oli St. James Town, in the island of St. Helena, your attention is directed to an enormous ladder, that extends from the town beneath to 8111) feet high. Previous to visiiing St. Helena 1 had heard much of tins immense ladder, and when at length 1 found myself on the spot, 1 resolved to ascend it. On inquiry, I found that sentinels were placed below and above, lor the purpose of preventing any one ascending or descending without an order from the Town Major. Together with a companion, alter dinner, I rambled down towards the guard house, and obtained an order to permit our ascent. The ladder is composed of steps better than three feel in width, and some four inches m breadth, firmly fastened in sides of great strength. On either side is a hand rail, of such a width that \ou can conveniently lay a hand on either side. The steps are each upwaids of 18 inches apart, and great numbers of them much decayed. At regular distances there are small seats for resting places fixed. Oil one side, without the ladder, a description of slide has been formed, along which puilies are fixed, for the purpose, it would seem, of raising anything from the town beneath, or lowering such from the fort above. The face of the hill against which the ladder is erected is extremely sleep so much so as to utterly preclude the idea of any ascent without artificial means; in places there are perfect precipices the rocks completely overhanging. At first we proceeded

rapidly, hut soon found that not to answer, the height of each step causing considerable exertion. More slowly, then, we moved along, till we attained the third resting place, where we seated ourselves, and turned to view the town beneath, covering, as it were, between the two mighty hills that seemed to press it on either side. As we attained a greater height, we found the steps getting more and more out ol repair, in some places two or three steps together, being broken so that we had to clamber up the best way we could. When we had reached within 100 feet or so ol the lop, au unusual fatigue almost

overpowered us; the dizzy height so affected us thai we felt as if we could scarce preserve ourselves from falling, yet we persevered and succeeded in reaching the top. A moment later, and one human being would have been passed iuto another world. My companion, who was before me, had scarcely passed tfie gate at the top, when he fainted, completely overcome, and he afterwards declared to me, that for the last hundred feet or so, nothing prevented his physical energies from being overcome, but the immediate prospect of reaching a place of safety. Many lives have been lost on this ladder, particularly those of passengers, whom curiosity induced to attempt the ascent. The artillerymen and garrison of the fort are, however, used to going up and down, exempt from casualties. Laddor Hill fort completely hangs over tfie bay; it is of great strength, and completely commands the roadstead beneath. In the batteries there are mounted generally eighteen 24 and 32 pounders, but there are some few guns of a larger calibre. 1 went to one of ttie batteries over the bay and looked beneath. The waters were below, and a little further out lay the shipping, looking like cock boats. A singular accident happened a few \eats previous on this very battery. A passenger from one of the ships in the hay had ascended to the fort, and looking Ironi the ramparts of one of the batteries, prerceived his vessel beneath, and thought lie could reach her w ith a stone, hut in his attempt to do so over-balanced himself, and fell from
the awful height, being dashed literally to pieces in the fall. After passing an hour at the fori we descended, but by the road, which is cut io a zig-zag manner in the side of the hills.

Address of a Child's Departed Spirit to its Parents. Kind parents why those tears ? And why those bursting sighs: No weeping here bedims Your little lov'd one's eyes.
The shade of eve you know Were hastening along, When my freed spirit left, To soar the stars among.
Yet long before the night Had drawn her veil around The home 1 left below, A better 1 had found.
So rapidly the soul Unbodied takes its fljght, That, scarce earth's scenery fail'd, When heaven's broke on niV sight.
Did not you, mother, see That bright celestial hand That smiled and beckoned me, And held th' inviting hand t
They let me stay awhile, To hear my mother pray, And see her close my eyes, And kiss th unconscious clay !
And then to heaven we þÿficw The cherubs led the way ; And as we soared I smiled As joyously as they.

Father ! I never knew 'Twas such a place as this, That heaven you told me of; So bright þÿ so full of bliss. Ob ' there is music here ! The softest, sweetest strains Float constantly along, O'er these ethereal plains.
List Mother þÿ Father, list ! A harp to me is given, And when I touch the strings, 'Tis heard all over heaven.
And shall I tell you who Stood ready to embrace Your little darling one, In tins most glorious place ?
'Twas Gran pa þÿ honord name! No more with age opprest, Or þÿtoil for in this world Are youth and endless rest.
His trembling voice is changed ; The trace of earthly cares Is banished from his cheek, And God has dried his tears.
Dear parents ! weep no more For those you lov'd so well, For glories here are ours, And joys, we may not teli.

One of the signs of the times" which in- " dicates the coiitinuauce, or rather the increase, of excitement on religious subjects throughout our fatherland, is the desire to celebrate the 300th anniversary of Luther's death, which, by whomsoever it may first have been expressed, now pervades all Germany. Our monarch has given permission for its being suitably commemorated throughout the Prussian dominions; Hanover has published a Consistorial circular to the eflect that, " as on the 18th of February next ensuing 300 years will have elapsed since Dr. Martin Luther exchanged time for eternity, all the clergy within our hounds are hereby called upon to improve the occasion from the pulpit on the following (Quinquagesima) Sunday, and more especially to seek, by their sermons on that day, to awaken or enliven in the hearts of their hearers feelings of grateful acknowledgment of what they owe to the agency of the blessed reformer, as well as In stir them up to a faithful adherence to their Lutheran confession " Brunswick. Wurtemberg, Detmolrl, the Hans Towns, and a variety of other places, have likewise announced their intention of celebrating this jubilee, which will no doubt he regarded as a sort of rallying point -and demonstration of Lutheran stiength and numbers þÿ London Paper.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger , London February 2, 1840. Terrible Disaster to the French in Algeria. By the French papers we learn that a fresh disaster has occurred to one of the detachments of the French army in the province of Coustantine, recalling the disaster of the retreat from Moscow. The column of General Levasseur was surprised on its return from a successful razzia in the mountains of the Boutaleb, province of Gonstaotioe, try a tremendous fall of snow. It was on the 2d of January that the column, consisting of about 2500 men, set out on its way back to the garrison of ISetif. The weather was beautiful, and the troops were marching in high spirits towards their bivouaes in the donuirs of their allies, the tribe of Msnoud, when, at about three in the afternoon, the sky became suddenly overcast, the snow began to fall, and chilled by a cold north wind, it soon reached the height of a foot and a hall The darkness was in a short time complete. The guides lost their way, and at five o'clock the soldiers bivouacked in the snow. Already had a part of the rearguard (alien victims to the severity of the weather, and the mules carrying the pro visions of the army having been unahle to proceed, the men remained frozen wuh cold and without food Un the morning of the 3d, the column resumed its maich. The snow still continued to lull, and the soldiers found the utmost dilficiilty in proceeding. All day they toiled on, advancing slowly. At midnight, however, they were si ill in the midst of a vast plain, dying from hunger and cold. þÿ was no country in the world with wlrrh

The guides had again lost the direction. þÿ They said they thought they were distant about three miles from the donairs of Msaoud, but, after seeking in vain for the road, they were obliged to give up all idea of finding it that night. Despair then took possession of the hearts of the men; disorder was at its height ; there was no shelter but a lew tents, the rest having been abandoned the day before. An immense number rushed pell mell into these tents, at the risk of sullocating each other; indeed, several thus met their next, both at the Vendue Office at þÿ10 2 deaths ; the rest of ihe column remained in the snow, which siill fell heavily, and waited till day light appeared, amidst the shrieks and lamentations of those who were dying every moment. Never had such a disaster been seen since the campaign of Bussia. Day at length dawned ; a great part of the men, with what remained of the baggage, began their march, the cavalry in front, towatds ISetif, distant about 25 miles ; this was the second day the soldiers bad tasted no food. þÿ The column became gradually thinner and longer, as the weakest lagged behind, and at every moment several fell down exhausted by the cold, whilst their comrades passed on. unahle to give them any assistance. At lour o'clock in the evening, the cavalry reached ISetif, and informed the inhabitants of the disaster which had taken place in the plain þÿ The garrison immediately turned out, and several of the inhabitants accompanied thcin

with carts, provisions, &e... to assist the unfortunate men lelt behind in the snow1. From that time till the 8th Jan. some soldiers were seen coming in led on horses, or brought in carriages by the inhabitants; but up to that period there were 806 men s'ill missing, many of whom will, no doubt, be saved ; but at present the loss in dead cannot be calculated, and the least exaggerated account is. that 100 men had died; but there is no doubt the number is great. Thirty officers have entered the hospital at Setif, with the extiemilies of their hands and feet frozen.

Translated from Le Manifesto Mai\ 1, The faults so frequently repeated by President Pierrot (unfortunately in defiance of the sage counsels of men sincerely devoted to their country) had for some time excited a lively inquietude in the public mind It had been hoped that the aged veteran would have ultimately comprehended the true wants of our Society, but, to no purpose þÿ lor every day, he persisted in compromising the future interests of the country. The Department of Artibonite, impatient to put an end to this intolerable state of things, gave the signal of insurrection, and pronounced the deposition of President Pierrot, and selected for his successor the General of Division Riche whose devotion to the maintenance of order was universally known. A deputation of the citizens of St. Marc, headed by General Jacques Louis arrived in this capital on yesterday afternoon (Saturday ) The intelligence circulated rapidly, and a large meeting of military chiefs, public functionaries, and private citizens assembled in the evening at the National palace, to which the Deputation had been conducted from the bureau of Aronilissement, but it was then resolved to defer until the day following the reception of the despatch. This morning, at the summons of the Commandant of the Department, the officers of the garrison of all grades, the public functionaries, and a great number of citizens assembled at the palace. The General Riche presented to the assembly the requisition

(still unopened) which had been addressed to him. After it had been read ; General Lazarre demanded of the assembly its opinion, how thev should act under such circumstances, and urged from all a free manifestation of their sentiments. Opinions were tendered pro ami con when General J. Louis having þÿ solicited permission to speak, said " Citizens of Port au Prince ! the citizens of A it þÿi bonite have confidence in you, they have made to you au appeal þÿ they await your decision. If you refuse to join them, they feel strong enough to act alone þÿ and are resolved one, and all to perish, il necessary in defence of their rights." These words decided the Assembly for with one voice, ' Vive le President liiche resounded throughout the meeting. Several voices exclaimed that they should refrain fram any acts which might tend to endanger the person of the fallen chief, and those suggestions were acceded to. General Riche then intimated that he could pot accept the trust of chief Magistrate of the State, until the assembly had decided on the rule of carrying on the regular action of the government. His ideas were based on the Constitution of 18 1(5, which was most applicable to the actual state of the country. Alter a short consultation between the chiefs of the different parties; the Constitution of lfilfl, was accepted þÿ to be hereafter modified in consonance with the experience acquired since 1843. The following Proclamation wcas immediately issued to the great satisfaction of the
country. liuuhty. equality. Republic of Hnyti. We, Jean Haptiste Riche, General of Division Ate. «Stc. ik.e.

r 8 2 02 A T 1 3. In presence of the General otficers, Colonels, and other officers of all grades of the garrison of Port au Prince ; the civil and judicial functionaries, and a uumeious assemblage of citizens of all ranks. After due consideration of the requisition addressed to us by the officers of the garrison and the citizens of L'Arlibonite þÿ and hearing the wishes so unanimously expressed by the citizens present, and confirmed bv the whole assembly, and moreover convinced by the arguments ol General Jacques Louis, speaking in the name of the citizens of L'Artibonite þÿ Faithful to the principles, and devoted to the interests of our country þÿ and feeling besides the necessity of guaranteeing the future by institutions, without which social order cannot exist ; and recognising in the integiiiy of the principles of the Constitution of 1810, under modifications as being alone applicable to the country, and attending at the same time an opportunity lor revising the social compact þÿ We Declare That on the principles following we will accept the charge as President ol Hayti, which we will thus administer; The Constitution of 1810 is restored in vigour with the exception ol the modification following þÿ 1. The privileges of the Legislative Assembly will be exercised aher the regulation of the decree of the 29th November 1841, by the Council of State which takes the title of Senate. Nevertheless, the mmitier of tins body will be limitled to 30, and its session will be ot three months annually, unless for

an extraordinary convocation. 2. The oliices of secretaries of Slate will continue. As soon as practicable, the Constitution of 1810 will be revised. Haitiens ! we will be ever united for- þÿ get the past þÿ and labour unanimously lor the welfare of our country. Done in the National Palace at Port au Prince, Mar. 1, 1840, and 43rd year of Independence. Other measures have also been adopted. þÿ A provisional council of secretaries of Slate has been formed. It is composed of; General Lazare President, with the Portfolio of war, General Deputy, marine and exterior relations; L. Rochel, of justice, and public instruction ; C. Ardouin, of the interior and agriculture ; J. Elic, of finance At commerce. A T IT S From the JSew York Herald, Match 3, 1840. Magnificent Knilrnad Projects. While government officials and babbling politicians are busily arranging and re arranging, tearing down, and tiuilomg up tariffs and systems of lortugu policy, (he master minds ol ihe age are contemplating ihu most inagmlicent enterprises that ever were con ceived, lor the advancement ot civilization, and the improvement of the condition ol the world. All the achievements ol science are vel to be surpassed, and greater ihings to be accomplished than were ever dreamed of in the most uiopiau philosophy of the last generation. Bands of iron are to clasp whole nations in a peaceful embrace, and and the new ties ol mutual interests to the common principles of their common humanity. The genius, the science, the enterprise, of the nineteenth centui v, are to usher m the tiisl drawing of a universal political inillenium. In llns great work of progression, the Arne i lean people are undoubtedly Ihe leaders It is natural that the free, democratic spirit of oui institutions, should incite and stimulate us to the loftiest undertakings ; and the influence of our example powerfully operates on the nations of Europe to follow. Great Britain, with the lorce of her military arid naval power, has struggled to open, lor her own advantage, the commercial resources of (Jhma. She has, with her sword, compelled that empire to annul its venerable policy of non intercourse ; but it lias been an unrighteous mode of bringing about uselul ends, and according to the natural laws ot compensation,

can never prosper. It is only just and bloodless, righteous and peaceful enterpiises, that result in permanent good, and this is eminently the American course of proceeding. It is the American possession of Oregon, and the vast commerce of that territory with the Chinese, carried on under the Ameiican flag, (which that singular race respect above all others,) that is gradually to teline and (Jims tianize Asia, and change the aspect of the woi Id. To make the Oregon effect all this þÿ to dovelope its mighty resources þÿ a railroad con nectiug the Mississippi valley with some point on the navigable part of the Columbia river, is absolutely necessary. For this purpose, various projects have been devised, and various routes selected, by Whitney, Wilkes, and others. The plan of Mr. Wilkes seems, in every respect, the most feasible, and we earnestly recommend it to the attention of the Federal Government. This ptoposition of a railroad to Oregon must not be regarded as chimerical. Starting, as Mr. Wilkes proposes, from the junction of the Great 1'latte with the Missouri, and following the level banks of the former river to its head, at the entrance of the South Pass, there can be no difficulty in the construction. Indeed, there is not a region ol country in the world; tiiat oilers lessobslruo lion to such a project. Why, then, should we delay? Why falter, at the outset? Every facility is in our hands. '1 he land already belongs to the government, and will cost nothing. The vast iron and coal regions of

Western Pennsylvania and Virginia, can end out their material by the wav of the Ohio aid Mississippi rivers; and anything else that is needed, New York, can send by the Lakes. The matter must not be procrastinated, or we shall be anticipated by our

great rival: and that which, in our hands, would enrich the whole Union, and tend to the high purposes of a true philanthropy, will become the ministering means, to the grasping avarice of some British company, of speculating capitalists. þÿW emake not this assertion. without good evidence ot its troth þÿ The following extract from the Royal Gazelle of January 2Nth, published at Frederickton in New Brunswick, will prove to our readers tiiat the British colonies are becoming alive to the subject ; and it will, doubtless, oon be introduced in Parliament. After giving an account of the American project, the Gazette says : þÿ þÿ Regarding the antagonist project of a British Nation at Railroad across our division of this continent, much as it may seem to deserve it, it is doubtful whether the time has not arrived when it may be too late to treat the language of the author of this pamphlet as the mere extravagance of a visionary. There is in it a point for consideration which can hardly fail eventually to have great weight in an estimate of the national importance of such a project. That railroads must give immensely increased facility and effect to both military and naval movements, as well as to civil enterprise, is perhaps, seriously doubted by no one ; and least of all is it doubted by the people of the United Slates. Perhaps no means of preparation for either defensive or aggressive operations could be devised, so well calculated at once to secure popularity at home, and to deprive foreign

powers of umbrage or ground of remonstrance. Whilst the ordinary army and navy need receive no apparent incre :se their effective force may be multiplied to indefinite extent by a system of internal improvement, having for its avowed or ostensible object no other than an increased facility of inland commerce and communication. But this is not þÿall. that expenditure which would be necessary for the extraordinary increase and subsequent maintenance of an army and navy, would afier the emergency had passed, remain a dead weight upon the country, in the form of an addition to the national debt and perhaps of permanent taxation ; but the same expenditure upon a judiciously planned railroad or svstem of roads, would, in ail probability, more than accomplish the same end, being in the mean lime, and afterwards continuing to be, instead of burthen, a growing source of revenue and sirength, with advantages directly recommending themselves as much to the poor as to the rich. þÿ Whether the Oregon question remain for solution by the last resort or not, none of the friends of peace on either side, can well object to the commercial and pacific contest of rival national railroads across this continent ; and, it may not be too much to say, that even should we retain, by amicable negociation, as much of the Oregon as we can desire, it will be held only by an unsafe tenure without the railroad. We have, at present, greatly the advantage of the United States in the proximity of

our own portion of this continent to Europe; but, it is plain that it would lose much of its value by delaying to turn it to account If the United States he the first tit effect a rail matt communication from the. Atlantic to the Tncific, hut a short time 'would he necessary to enable them to inundate the Oregon with emigrants under their protection, and thus greatly to prejudice, if not wholly to atmthi

jtMBwn.n- þÿI 'mk late, British influence there. Besiiles, by the front that they would thus present towards India and China, a double influence would also be at their command, tending to dim o through their own avenues, the trade of the Canadas either to the Atlantic or the Pacific, and eventually to absorb the Canadas themselves. So natural is this apparent tendency of railroad communication, existing and pro. jected in the United States, that it seems to be a question, the decision of which cannot be safe to rely for the arrest of such tendency upon any thing short of a similar and countervailing tendency of greater force. A British railroad from the coast of Nova Scotia, through the Canadas to the Pacific, with necessary branches, seems the most naturally to present even more than such a desideratum. Besides most acceptably establishing in the Canadas an interest separate and truly British, and stronger than that inclining towards the United States, such a road would also rather attract the trade and communication of the latter through the Canadas, by affording a more regular and rapid intercourse with Europe than could possibly he maintained from any point of the Union.' How jealous is this writer of the idea of the American project being carried into execution ! How clearly does he see the infinite superiority it would give us over everv other power in the world, and particularly over Great Britain! Ii is a hold project, a mass teilv project, and John Bull will spend his last guinea to beat it if he can,

But another rival has sprung np in this matter of engrossing the vast trade of China and the East Indies. On looking over our late file uf French papers, we find that it is proposed by the Russian government to extend to Pekin, in China, the line of railroad which is now in course of construction between St. Petersburg and Moscow. And it is probable that some sort of negociattons have already taken place between the Russians and Chinese, or, perhaps, the Tartars on the borders of the two nations, in regard to the project. Every one who has an ade. quate idea of the resources of Russia, and the absolute power of its Czar, will admit its practicability What work is it impossible for the Emperor to perform, with twenty million serfs at his immediate þÿcommand the slaves of his will f Where Could we find so numerous or cheap a body of laborers to carry on this great enterprise? In this respect we cannot compete with Russia, nor can Great Britain. It might, however, be a great inducement to laborers, should a pro, mise of a grant of land along the route be held out to all who worked upon it a Certain time. Yet, in every thing but mere labor, we infinitely surpass all our competitors. We have greater skill, more indomitable energv, and a suit of go-ahead spirit that nothing can equal. Thus then, do we stand at present. Great Britain. Russia, and the United States, are all at the same time entertaining projects for securing a rapid communication with Chinn, Northwest America, and the East Indies.

Which has the most enterprise, time will show. We trust, for the honor and welfare of our country, that Congress will not neglect to give this matter a candid consideration. I.et the people, on all hands, assemble and petition their representatives to awake from their slumber, and not stand idly by while

s tr» e at a si a v « 3 foreign governments are taking steps to reap the harvest that should be ours. Above all, let the mercantile Community of New York remember, that the execution of this project may render our city the emporium of the Commerce of the world.

From Hell's Weekly Messenger, London. February 2!3, 1846. a ARRIVAL OF THE INDIAN MAIL. Tim particulars which we have given in another column of one of the most bloody conflicts which ever look place upon the soil o! India, will be read with a deep and painful interest. The viciory was on the side of the British; But it was a victory dearly purchased, no less than sixty one gallant officers having fallen, and upwards of 3000 of our brave troops being k . I led or wounded. Airn-ii g ihe officers who fell we find the names of the hero of Jellalabad, the gallant Sir Hubert Sale; Major Gen. Sir John þÿM Caskil! ; Major Broadfoot, the political agent; Lieut. Col. J. B. Wood, aide de camp to ihe Governor |General ; Lieut. Col. Gough, and Major Gen. F. Somerset, military secretaries to ihe Commander in Chief and Governor General. The forces actually engaged amounted, on the part of the British, to 20,000 : on that of the Sikhs, to 60,000. The (ire of the enemy ris stated to have been tremendous ; indeed the heavy losses we have suffered sufficiently attest tbe fact. The Governor General and the Commander in Chief were in the thickest of tfie fight, and Sir Henry Hardinge, who had placed himself under the orders of Sir Hugh Gough, led on a division, heading a charge, and carrying an important position. The defeated army of the Sikhs retreated to the Sutlej, which, it is reported, they ctossed on the 29th of December.

The Spanish Ministry. þÿ The accounts received from Madrid during the last few davs have possessed more than usual interest It appears that, owing to some differences of opinion in the Cabiuct respecting the mar-

tlage of the young Queen with Count Trapani an intrigue was set on foot by the Queen Motheh, seconded by General Narvaez, to get rid of those members of the Cabinet who had opposed that measure. The first step was the resignation of Narvaez, under the pretence tlmt his health was failing him. This resignation was accepted by the Queen, who then sent for the Marquis de Viluma, and asked him to undertake the reconstruction of the Cabinet. The Marquis represented that his political opinions rendered it impossible to comply With the request, but as her Majesty insisted, he accepted the commission. Having failed in his attempt to form a Cabinet he again waited on the Queen, and urged her Majesty to recall the Duke of Valencia, the only man, in his opinion, who could extricate the government from its critical position The five colleagues of General Narvaez, in the meantime, came to the resolution of continuing in office until dismissed by the Sovereign. Their motive for adopting that resolution was that her Majesty had told M. Martinez de la Rosa, in announcing to him the resignation of General Narvaez, that the Cabinet was de facto dissolved, which they Considered tantamount to a dismissal, and as the Cortes had on no occasion denied them its support, they did not think proper voluntarily to retire The Queen again sent for General Narvaez, who, after, resisting a while, consented to accept the mission of composing a new Cabinet. In this attempt he appears to have (ailed, hut he was suc-

cessful in procuring the dismissal ot bis lale colleagues. After some further difficulty a ministry was formed, the various offices being filled up as follows: þÿ General Nat \ nez, General in Chief of the army: the Marquis de Miraflores, President of the Council, Minister ot Foreign Affairs; M. Istuiitz, Minister of the Interior; General Roncali, Minister of War ; Admiral Popete, Minister of Marine; M. Lorenzo A razola, Minister of Justice It only remained to appoint the Minister of Finance, and it was generally supposed that M. Casa liitra, one of the richest capitalists of Madrid would be named. It is generally believed that the new Cabinet is merely a provisional one. þÿ Lon. don Paper, February 23.

Suit wkkCk off Bout, home. þÿ We learn front Boulogne sur-Mer, that about five o'clock in tiie afternoon of Saturday last, after a most tempestuous day, an English sloop, with a crew of five men, leaking at every plank attempted to make that port, hut, from want of sufficient depth ol water to get in, was obliged to run aground to the cast of t he pier, a short distance from the stockade. The life boat was immediately launched, hut, though stoutly manned, and three attempts made to reach the vessel, they were defeated, till at the last it was dashed hack again, upon the beach, and so much damaged as to be rendered unserviceable (or a lime. Not discouraged by this defeat Meguin, a pilot, made an effort, with some resolute fellows, to get off with his boat, but such was the force of the waves that ihcy found it impossible to advance. Notwithstanding this second failure, Testard, the owner of a fishing boat which was new and strongly built, resolved to brave the danger, and with bis men. bv bold and skilful management. got out of t tic harbour, and, although it took them an hour to get over the few yatds

ST, A'TIS. that separated them from the vessel aground, t they reached it, and found the men lashed to the masts. Testard took with him a small boat to bring the men from (be vessel on board his own smack It was put out, and three of the snlibrers got into it, but a moment after the little boat was upset, and two of the three men were drowned. The third being a good swimmer, reached the smack, and was taken in. Testard was obliged to put back from t fie loss ot the boat, leaving 1 tie other two men ou the sloop. Seeing this and that the storm slightly abated, the cornmis de marine, M. Platrier, took another boat, and witli his men reached the vessel, and brought t he two men away. The revolution which took place on the 1st March and which has established in vigor and force the Constitution of 1816, wiih some modifications, and the elevation ol General Riche to the Presidency ol the Reputilic, was entirely in favour of persons and properties. It is well known, as History attests, that revolutions always threaten to effect social innovations. We have had to deplore since 1843, the tendency of our society to deviale from the principles which brought about the events of that year, and to plunge into extremes the consequences of which might have proved fatal to our counliy. Society badly directed would have been disorganised, where should we have arrested the evil without the revolution which has given to us the Constitution of 1816 ? Truly one must acknowledge that there is the ability in General Riche to give us that guarantee. To convince þÿone s elf of that truth, let us see what has happened at Leogane, Jacmel, Connives, at .Mirebalais, and at Laschobas, eveiv where in þÿtact, where the population has been called on to express freely its opinion. As an electric fire, the word Constitution has sufficed lor the people to adhere unanimously to what had occurred at St Marc and Port au Prince. Is not the unanimity of the people in these movements to be plainly seen? We abstain from reflections on this subject ; facts speak, and will yet speak. As soon as Gen. T. Denis at Gonaives had received i lie act of acceptation of the new President, be

hesitated no longer; but convoked the principal citizens and chiefs ol the garrison and laid before them the communication. The whole were of accord to second the movements of St. Marc, and Port mi Prince. A process verbal was immediately drawn up to ratify this adhesion; it was covered with signatures. The Generals Stanislaus Linding, Simon, E Moreau, and Brice hastened from the ('ape, to march the garrison of Gonaives against St. Marc. These ofiicets were in the first instance arrested, but afterwards liberated and sent to the Cape. Nevertheless, the authorities of Gonaives had despatched troops to the frontiers of that Department to provide against any attack on the part of President Pierrot, if in his blindness he should attempt an) move

merit against Gonaives. From Si Mate, a battalion of the 7th þÿ another of the 8ih and a squadron of cavalry were sent to Gonaives to support the resistance of that place The first regiment was moved to þÿL Aicahh a d will advance if it prove necessary. At Leogone. Jacmel, Mirebelais, and Lascahohas the Generals Therlonge, Casunir, Augustin and Gefliard have behaved admirably, they have likewise been well supported by ihe officers under their command. The adhesion of the populations of the Departments has been unanimous and spontaneous, and measures have been taken as well for the maintenance of order, as the secuiity of their frontiers. The troops ot the V'ereties and of Petit Riviere were defiled in the direction by which their quarters were most likely to be invaded. The General J. Gillies Gonave at JVlarband has taken steps to resist any aggressions on the part of the fallen authority. Provisions and munitions of war have b en sent from St. Marc to Gonaives and Ft tit Goive, where General S. Telemaque is with the 24ih regt. and a great number ol National Guards. A:de de camps have been despatch ed by sea to Jeren.ie, þÿL Anse þÿd Hnvnaiilt, Mole and to Port a Paix, to carry (he intelligence of ihe new revolution to the inhabitants of those quarters. information we have procured. From the St Thomas Times, April 18, 1846. We have Irom lime to time called the attention of our readers to various matters which we deemed worthy the especial consideration of those whose position in tins community can euahle them to carry into execution a social improvement. That oui success has not been commensurate wait the earnestness of our efforts we are constrained to admit, but as it is a pleasing duly we again essay it. and recommend the establishment of a Bank of Deposit for small sums, the savings of the humbler classes. !Su It an Institution though it must he unattended wiih profit, would he productive of great benelit. Wherever one has been established we lind that the thrifty and saving have avail d themselves of its advantages; þÿ habits f economy and fore thought have been generated and waste and dissipation check d. An institution of the kind, induces many, who would otherwise be improvident, to accumulate a provision for sickness, old age, or burial, which renders them independent of eleemosynary aid. In that point of view it is worthy the attention of tiie rich, whilst higher motives should actuate the philantropic. Believing as we do, that a Hank for Savings is much required in this city for the accommodation of those of limited means, we hope that having brought the subject ihus publicly foiward, it will be speedily and efficiently taken up. it only requires a few influential and public spirited gentlemen to give the impetus, and success is certain. þÿ oo> þÿ From Bell's H eehly Messenger, London

Match 30, 1816. Spain þÿ The intelligence from this country is of great importance. The Miraffores Cabinet has through a coup d'etat of General Narvnez. been overthrown, and another inaugurated under the auspices of lhat ambitious general. The character of the new Cabinet, and ihe course which it intends to pursue, nwv he gathered from the (act that as soon as it was installed, two decrees were issued, þÿ one proroguing the Cortes to an indefinite period, the other virtually suspending the liberty ol the press. The new ministry have issued a long manifesto to the Spanish nation, in which they denounce the periodical press as a coniinii.nl source of scandal, and a torch flung each day into ilie midst of society to reduce it to ashes. In the decree against the press we find the following sweeping articles : þÿ "Art. I. Attacks and offensive expressions against my royal person, or against niv family, or against loieign sovereigns, or the princes or their families, or against the constitution and laws of ihe country, or against the free exercise of my constitutional prerogatives, or against the present decree, before it is judged by the Cortes, shall lie punished by the immediate suppression of the journal so offending. "Art. 2. Attacks against public functionaries. whether relative to the acts of their private life, or malevolently attributing to them evil intentions in their official acts, shall lie punished wiih the temporary suspen-ionof the journal, " Art. 3. Such writings as shall have for

object to excite to disobedience or to bring lire government and its measures into contempt shall irieur the same penalty." In the present temper of lite Spanish nation, it is too much to expect that such a despotic system will be quietly submitted to We mnv, therefore, soon expect to hear of fresh disturbances, civil and military pro nouncerneiits, and those frightful massacres and summary executions which are theii invariable concomitants.

Latest from Poland. We regret to find that the peasantry in tjalli'cis suit continue to perpetrate the rtiost cruel atrocities! the Austrian and Russian governments are taking active and vigorous measures to put a stop to their bat ba'rities. According to the Warsaw Courier, several of the ringleaders in the late revolt have been tried by a court martial : three were sentenced to be hanged, and others to be banished to Siberia, the whole of their property being Confiscated. One of the three on whom sentence of death Was passed has been respited ; the others were executed. By virtue of an arrangement concluded between the three Powers, General Gount Wrbna has taken, under certain provisions, the command of the free city of Cracow lor three rears. It is said that at the expiration of that time, and after each successive term of three years, the protecting Powers will in turn name a military commandant. The free city of Cracow will thus be treated in the same manner as the fortress of Mayence. þÿ Belt's Weekly Messenger, Marsh 30, 18 Hi.

IMPORTANT FROM PORTUGAL. The arrival of the steam-ship Queen at Southampton has put us in possession of letters and papers of a late date from Portugal. The Queen brought home about 90 persons, passengers, including the crew and passengers of the Great Liverpool. They are in a very distressed condition for want of clothing nnd many other necessaries. It is with extreme regret that we announce the death of Captain M'Leod. the late commander of the Great Liverpool, who died by his own hand immediately after the last of the passengers bad departed from Corunna He had been in a most desponding state of mind ever since the unfortunate occurrence, and it is supposed could not bear up against misfortune. He was a man universally beloved and respected, and has left a large young family, with prospects of an early increase, Lieut. Williamson, the Admiralty agent of the Great Liverpool, lies dangerously ill at Corumia ; so much so, that tiis life is despaired of. In one respect apart from nil others, the news which arrived by t tie I oronlo is ol considerable importance. We have been too long accustomed t<> hear of British wars and aggressions in the Bast, that we are apt to view with indifference any thing coming from that quarter. But at the present time> when a war between America and Great Britain may not be an improbable event, any thing that concerns the prosperity or adversitv of England is of some importance to us, and we cannot fail to be interested. In this view, the war of the Punjaub, which has broken out with tremendous violence, is calculated to arrest the attention of our statement and it may, perchance materially affect the pending negotiations between England nnd America Letters received in England by the overland mail, state that " the Sikhs attacked the British army with fifty five thousand men. ami 130 pieces of artillery, on the 2 1 st of December. The Sikhs are very powerful, supported hy an active and brave people, and are goaded on to vengeance by the continual aggressions which have been ihade upon them by the British in their relentless policV of aggrandisement or annexation Not content with the vast possessions she already has in India, Great Britain looks with a longing eve, on the fertile regions of the IVmjmib, and will never satisfy her rapacity Until she swallows up every neighbouring power in that section of the globe. But a short time lias elapsed since she forcibly annexed Natal to her African colonies, on a

plea of a philanthropy : but really fol the value of the country, for the production of cotton ; and now siie seeks to annex the Punjaub to her territory by the liloo.lv power of the sword. Yet this is the nation whose presses, whose pulpits, whose parliamentary orators, have the felicity to abuse us lor the peaceful and bloodless annexation ol I exas, by the free consent and desire ol the people. The bold system of resistance which the Sikhs have manifested, although urged on b_V England, leads us to believe that the permanent annexation of their territory will he no very easy matter ; no easier, perhaps, than the permanence of the French possessions in Algetia There seems to be every probability that England will have to contend against a force equally as determined as any in Affghanislan s at any rate, there will be such difficulties thrown in her way bv the gallant Sikhs as to give full employment to her arms, and to weaken her capacity somewhat for carrying on a war with the United States She is aware that we are now too powerful to cope with while she has other nations to battle with or subdue ; and. in this view, this fresh outbreak in, and near her East India possessions, may have its effect on the negotiation for the settlement ol the Oregon question. This news is likelv to have an influence in leading to the peaceable adjustment of the Oregon question. It may tend to weaken the persistence of Great Britain in maintaining her pretensions, and strengthen our go-
vernment in the assertion of our rights W e shall see. It will not lie the fnsi time at all events, that troubles in India have had an influence on negotiations between England and America.

The WiI.d Cattle of Texas þÿ The settlers who have recently opened farms near the sources of the San Gabriel and Brushy, find the country well stocked with a singular breed of wild cattle. Large droves ol these catile are found not only on the San Gabriel, Leona, and other tributaries of Little Kiver, but also on the San Saba, the Llaho, and many tributaiies of the Upper Colerado, lur above the settlements. They differ in form, colour, and habits from all the varieties of domestic cattle in Texas. Tliey are invariably of a dark brown colour, with a slight tinge of dusky yellow on the tip ol the nose and the belly. Their horns are remarkably large, and stand out straight from the head. Although these cattle are generally much larger than the domestic cattle, they are more fleet and nimble, and when pursued, ollen outstrip horses that easily outrun the buffalo t thev seldom venture far out into the prairies, but are generally found in or near the forests that skirt the streams in that section. Their meal is of an excellent flavour, and is prelerred by the settlers to the meat of the domestic cattle. It is said that their lat is so hard and compact that it will not melt in the hottest days of summer, and the Candles formed with it aie far superior to those that are formed with the tailow <d other cattle. Some persons have supposed that it is possible these cattle are a distinct race, indigenous to America ; and the immense skeleton ol a species of fossil ox, with straight horns, that

are often found in the beds of the Brazos and Colerado would seem to strengthen this opinion. But as these cattle are now found oniv in the vicinity of the old missions, it is much more probable that they are the descendants of the cattle introduced by the early Spanish adventurers. These cattle are so wild that they can only be caught olive by entrapping them in disguised pits. The celebrated botanist, Douglas while on a tour in one of those islands, fell into one of these pits, and was gored to death by a wild bull, who had been thus entrapped. Several attempts have been made by the settlers on the San Gabriel to domesticate the wild cattle in that section, but they have thus far been unsuccessful. As they are far superior to the domestic cattle of the Country, not only in size, strength, ami agility, but also in the flavour of their meat, and the density of their fat, thev might, if once domesticated, become a valuable acquisition to the agriculturists of the country Houston Telegraph.
Aneciiotf.s of a Newfoundland Dog þÿ We ourselves possessed a dog of this species, that, upon a night attack of burglars, broke

... i i . > n his chain, scoured through a long yard in which he was kept, and, taking an enormous leap upwards, Caught hold of a lelloW by the tail of his coat, who was entering the window of a conservatory on the first floor, and brought down the flaps between his teeth. Nor did this trophy content him ; for, utterly disdaining a bit of poisoned meat thrown at him, he pointed and yelped at the thief, till the alarm was given and the fellow discovered. The same dog permitted a robin, through a whole winter, to take shelter in his den. It was a most singular spectacle to witness; for so much familiarity, and, as it seemed affection, grew Up between them, that, while robin hopped and chirped about between his shaggy paws, or upon his head and body, our Newfoundland would stand or lie perfectly still, his small brown eyes winking and blinking, and his well clothed tail gently wagging to and fro with satisfaction. A feat of this dog deserves commemoration. A boy, belonging to the house, had not returned home at the usual hour, to the great alarm of his neither. The dog above mentioned, seeming to share in the general disturbance, followed the servant, sent in one direction, to seek out the truant ; but soon distanced and lost sight of him, and was the first to discover the boy's apparel on the water's edge, and, a few minutes after, the boy himself in the river, who was then sinking. The noble animal plunged in and rescued the child, who, it appeared, had tun off with his elder brother's Corks, and being of a

determined and independent character, had ventured to swim by himself. At the moment of time of the dog's approach, he had got embarrassed and entangled iu his machinery, and must ccitaiiiiv have been drowned hut for this timely assistance. --Craven's liecreations in Shooting.

ANOTHER CHANCE IN THE SPA- NISH MINISTRY. The Journal des Debuts of Wednesday publishes the following important news from Spain : þÿ þÿ We have received intelligence from Madrid to the 4th of April. A new ministerial crisis has arisen, hut in less than 24 hours it arrived at a commencement of solution. It was already known that two members of the Cabinet, M. Egana, Minister of Grace and Justice, and General Peznela, Minister of Marine, not finding themselves in accord with their colleagues with respect to an ordinance relative to the Stock Exchange had resigned. General þÿI ezuela, who was to have countersigned that ordinance, was replaced during day the of the 3d of April by

General Mazarredo. The latter, formerly chief officer on the staff of General Narvaez, was personally devoted to him tVl, Gonzales Bravo, for whom the Portfolio of Foreign A flairs was destined, not only would not accept it, but resigned his appointment of Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of Lisbon He is said to have notified his resignation in the most energetic terms, and by proclaiming loudly that he remained faithful to a liberal course of policy. þÿ It remained, therefore, to provide for the functions of Minister for Foreign Affairs, and to replace M. Egana. General Narvaez, after having in vain attempted to complete his ministry, determined on the morning of the 4th of April to resign. The Queen accepted his resignation, and immediately summoned M. Isturitz. to inti ust to him t; e mission of forming a new Cabinet. M. Isturitz hastened to comply with the Queen's wishes. ! le was appointed President nt he Council and Minister for Foreign Attairs. General Artnero, who during the first ministry of Narvaez remained to the last united witli his tlnee colleagues, M M. Mon, Pinal, and Mayans, was appointed Minister of Marine. It was said, at the departure of the courier from Madrid, that it was expected likewise that M. Mon would resume (tie Portfolio of Finance, and that he would give to the Isturits Cabinet the aid of his rare capacity and of his rigid probity. It was likewise thought that M. Pidal, who joined so zealously in all the financial reforms of M. Mon, and who has already introduced

into the country some important adttiimstialive ameliorations, would enter the new Cabinet M. Egana lias consented to retain the Portfolio ol Grace and Justice. 'The new President of the Council, M, Isturitz, has already been at the head of a ministry, in the difficult period which preceded t lie revolution of La Grauja. He w is Minister of the Interior in ihe last Cabinet of M. M nurtures. We have received letters dated Bayonne 5th inst, announcing that the Infante Don Enrique had arrived the preceding day in the port of St' Jean de Luz, onboard the Spanish ship of war the Constitucion. It is known that the late Narvaez ministry had requested the young prince, who was at Corunna, to proceed to travel þÿabroad.
